newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Soros sees no panic if Italy, Spain miss EMU date.
newsitem.headline: Soros sees no panic if Italy, Spain miss EMU date.

text.p: Hungarian-born financier George Soros said on Monday that markets need not panic if Italy and Spain missed the start of European monetary union.
He also backed Britain's wait-and-see stance on membership.

Soros, credited with having almost single-handedly driven the British pound out of the Echange Rate Mechanism -- Europe's currency grid -- in 1992, said differences between the British and Continental economies counselled caution on the single currency.
"To rush in might be dangerous," he said at the World Economic Forum, an annual meeting of top political leaders and businessmen.

Soros said that financial markets, which have been betting heavily on Spain, Italy and Portugal being in monetary union at the launch on January 1, 1999, might react calmly even if they missed the cut providing it was clear that they would form part of a second wave of entrants.
"If you have a firm commitment that (they will) be in the second round, then the effect on the bond market could be quite mild," Soros said.
Soros, who heads a multi-billion dollar investment fund, said he believed that European states would meet the launch date for monetary union because any delay "would be catastrophic."

Even if Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) was a flawed plan, because many of the EU's 15 states had unresolved economic problems, he said the political will to wed member economies in the single currency was overwhelming.
"We are going to have it (EMU) on January 1, 1999...I believe the political decision has been made (to go ahead)," he told a news conference at this Swiss mountain resort.

Soros, who refused to answer any questions about his investment strategies, echoed one of the dominant themes of the conference -- that the labour market in many European countries was too rigid, causing continuing high unemployment.

The financier, whose words can move financial markets, said it was one of the ironies of the Maastricht Treaty -- the blueprint for monetary union -- that budgetary restraints prevented governments lowering the taxes that companies had to pay for their employees, one measure which could help boost employment.
But while the British were probably right to wait beyond January 1, 1999, before joining, indefinitely delaying membership of a single currency could be damaging for its economy, Soros said.

Echoing a recent warning by a leading Japanese businessman, Soros said that Britain had gained much by being a bridge for non-EU investors -- particularly from Japan and the U.S. -- to sell into mainland Europe and this advantage would be lost if it stayed out permanently.
